{{Short description|On all absolute values of rational numbers}}
In [[number theory]], '''Ostrowski's theorem''', due to [[Alexander Ostrowski]] (1916), states that every non-trivial [[absolute value (algebra)|absolute value]] on the [[rational number]]s <math>\Q</math> is equivalent to either the usual real absolute value or a [[p-adic number|{{mvar|p}}-adic]] absolute value.<ref name="ThmStatement">{{cite book |last=Koblitz |first=Neal |authorlink=Neal Koblitz |title=P-adic numbers, p-adic analysis, and zeta-functions |year=1984 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=New York |isbn=978-0-387-96017-3 |url=https://www.springer.com/mathematics/numbers/book/978-0-387-96017-3 |edition=2nd |accessdate=24 August 2012 |page=3 |quote='''Theorem 1''' (Ostrowski). Every nontrivial norm ‖ ‖ on <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> is equivalent to {{math|{{abs|&nbsp;}}<sub>''p''</sub>}} for some prime {{mvar|p}} or for <math>p=\infty</math>.|series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics }}</ref>

== Theorem statement ==
An '''absolute value''' on the rational numbers is a function <math>|\cdot|_*: \Q \to \R</math> satisfying for all <math>x, y\in\mathbb{Q}</math> 
# <math>|x|_* \ge 0</math>, with equality [[if and only if]] <math>x = 0</math>
# <math>|xy|_* = |x|_* |y|_*</math>
# <math>|x + y|_* \le |x|_* + |y|_*</math>

Two absolute values <math>|\cdot|</math> and <math>|\cdot|_*</math> on the rationals are defined to be '''equivalent''' if they induce the same [[Topological space|topology]]; this can be shown to be equivalent to the existence of a positive [[real number]] <math>\lambda \in (0, \infty)</math> such that

: <math>|x|_* = |x|^\lambda</math>

for all rational <math> x </math>. (Note: In general, if <math>|x|</math> is an absolute value, <math>|x|^\lambda</math> is not necessarily an absolute value anymore; however ''if'' two absolute values are equivalent, then each is a positive power of the other.<ref>Schikhof (2007) Theorem 9.2 and Exercise 9.B</ref>) The '''trivial absolute value''' on any field ''K'' is defined to be

: <math>|x|_0 := \begin{cases} 0, & x = 0, \\ 1, & x \ne 0. \end{cases}</math>

The '''real absolute value''' on the [[rational numbers|rationals]] <math>\Q</math> is the standard [[absolute value]] on the reals, defined to be

: <math>|x|_\infty := \begin{cases} x, & x \ge 0, \\ -x, & x < 0. \end{cases}</math>

This is sometimes written with a subscript 1 instead of [[infinity]].

For a [[prime number]] {{mvar|p}}, the [[P-adic absolute value|{{mvar|p}}-adic absolute value]] on <math>\Q</math> is defined as follows: any non-zero rational {{mvar|x}} can be written uniquely as <math>x = p^n \tfrac{a}{b}</math>, where {{mvar|a}} and {{mvar|b}} are [[coprime integers]] not divisible by {{mvar|p}}, and {{mvar|n}} is an integer; so we define

: <math>|x|_p := \begin{cases} 0, & x = 0, \\ p^{-n}, & x, \ne 0. \end{cases}</math>

Ostrowski's theorem then states that if <math>|\cdot|_*: \Q \to \R</math> is any absolute value on the rational numbers, then either <math>|\cdot|_* = |\cdot|_0</math>, or <math>|\cdot|_*</math> is equivalent to <math>|\cdot|</math>, or <math>|\cdot|_*</math> is equivalent to <math>|\cdot|_p</math>.<ref name="ThmStatement"/>

== Proof ==
The following proof follows the one of Theorem 10.1 in Schikhof (2007).

Let <math>|\cdot|_*</math> be an absolute value on the rationals. We start the proof by showing that it is entirely determined by the values it takes on [[Prime number|prime numbers]].

From the fact that <math>1 \times 1 = 1</math> and the multiplicativity property of the absolute value, we infer that <math>|1|_*^2 = |1|_*</math>. In particular, <math>|1|_*</math> has to be 0 or 1 and since <math>1 \neq 0</math>, one must have <math>|1|_* = 1</math>. A similar argument shows that <math>|-1|_* = 1</math>. 

For all [[Natural number|positive integer]] {{mvar|n}}, the multiplicativity property entails <math>|-n|_* = |-1|_* \times |n|_* = |n|_*</math>. In other words, the absolute value of a negative integer coincides with that of its opposite.

Let {{mvar|n}} be a positive integer. From the fact that <math>n^{-1} \times n = 1</math> and the multiplicativity property, we conclude that <math>|n^{-1}|_* = |n|_*^{-1}</math>.

Let now {{mvar|r}} be a positive rational. There exist two [[Coprime integers|coprime]] positive integers {{mvar|p}} and {{mvar|q}} such that <math>r = p q^{-1}</math>. The properties above show that <math>|r|_* = |p|_* |q^{-1}|_* = |p|_* |q|_*^{-1}</math>. Altogether, the absolute value of a positive rational is entirely determined from that of its numerator and denominator.

Finally, let <math>\mathbb{P}</math> be the set of prime numbers. For all positive integer {{mvar|n}}, we can write

: <math>n = \prod_{p \in \mathbb{P}} p^{v_p(n)},</math>

where <math>v_p(n)</math> is the [[p-adic valuation]] of {{mvar|n}}. The multiplicativity property enables one to compute the absolute value of {{mvar|n}} from that of the prime numbers using the following relationship

: <math>|n|_* = \left| \prod_{p \in \mathbb{P}} p^{v_p(n)} \right|_{*} = \prod_{p \in \mathbb{P}} |p|_*^{v_p(n)}.</math>

We continue the proof by separating two cases:

# There exists a positive integer {{Mvar|n}} such that <math>|n|_* > 1</math>; or
# For all integer {{Mvar|n}}, one has <math>|n|_* \leq 1</math>.

=== First case ===
Suppose that there exists a positive integer {{Mvar|n}} such that <math>|n|_* > 1.</math> Let {{Mvar|k}} be a non-negative integer and {{Mvar|b}} be a positive integer greater than <math>1</math>. We express <math>n^k</math> in [[Radix|base]] {{Mvar|b}}: there exist a positive integer {{Mvar|m}} and integers <math>(c_i)_{0 \leq i < m}</math> such that for all {{Mvar|i}}, <math>0 \leq c_i < b</math> and <math>n^k = \sum_{i<m} c_i b^i</math>. In particular, <math>n^k \ge b^{m-1}</math> so <math>m \leq 1 + k \log_b n</math>.

Each term <math>|c_i b^i|_*</math> is at most <math>(b - 1) |b|_*^i</math>. (By the multiplicative property, <math>|c_i b^i|_* = |c_i|_* |b|_*^i</math>, then using the fact that <math>c_i</math> is a digit, write <math>c_i = 1 + 1 + \cdots + 1</math> so by the triangle inequality, <math>|c_i| \le |1| + |1| + \cdots + |1| = c_i \le b - 1</math>.) Besides, <math>|b|_*^i</math> is at most <math>\max\{1, |b|_*^{m-1}\}</math>. By the triangle inequality and the above bound on {{Mvar|m}}, it follows:
: <math>\begin{align}
|n|_*^k & \leq m \max_{i<m} \{|c_i b^i|_*\} \\
        & \leq m (b - 1) \max \{1, |b|_*^{m-1}\} \\
        & \leq (1 + k \log_b n) (b - 1) \max\{1, |b|_*^{k \log_b n}\}.
\end{align}</math>

Therefore, raising both sides to the power <math>1/k</math>, we obtain

: <math>|n|_* \leq \left((1 + k \log_b n) (b - 1)\right)^{1/k} \max \{1, |b|_*^{\log_b n}\}.</math>

Finally, taking the limit as {{Mvar|k}} tends to infinity shows that

: <math>|n|_* \leq \max \{1, |b|_*^{\log_b n}\}.</math>

Together with the condition <math>|n|_* > 1,</math> the above argument leads to <math>|b|_* > 1</math> regardless of the choice of {{Mvar|b}} (otherwise <math>|b|_*^{\log_b n} \leq 1</math> implies <math>|n|_* \leq 1</math>). As a result, all integers greater than one have an absolute value strictly greater than one. Thus generalizing the above, for any choice of integers {{Mvar|n}} and {{Mvar|b}} greater than or equal to 2, we get

: <math>|n|_* \leq |b|_*^{\log_b n},</math>

i.e.

: <math>\log_n |n|_* \leq \log_b |b|_*.</math>

By symmetry, this inequality is an equality. In particular, for all <math>n \geq 2</math>, <math>\log_n |n|_* = \log_2 |2|_* = \lambda</math>, i.e. <math>|n|_* = n^\lambda = |n|_\infty^\lambda</math>. Because the [[triangle inequality]] implies that for all positive integers {{mvar|n}} we have <math> |n|_* \leq n</math>, in this case we obtain more precisely that <math>0 < \lambda \leq 1</math>.

As per the above result on the determination of an absolute value by its values on the prime numbers, we easily see that <math>|r|_* = |r|_\infty^\lambda</math> for all rational {{Mvar|r}}, thus demonstrating equivalence to the real absolute value.

=== Second case ===
Suppose that for all integer {{Mvar|n}}, one has <math>|n|_* \leq 1</math>. As our absolute value is non-trivial, there must exist a positive integer {{Mvar|n}} for which <math>|n|_* < 1.</math> Decomposing <math>|n|_*</math> on the prime numbers shows that there exists <math>p \in \mathbb{P}</math> such that <math>|p|_* < 1</math>. We claim that in fact this is so for one prime number only.

Suppose ''[[Reductio ad absurdum|by way of contradiction]]'' that {{Mvar|p}} and {{Mvar|q}} are two distinct primes with absolute value strictly less than 1. Let {{Mvar|k}} be a positive integer such that <math>|p|_*^k</math> and <math>|q|_*^k</math> are smaller than <math>1/2</math>. By [[Bézout's identity]], since <math>p^k</math> and <math>q^k</math> are [[coprime]], there exist two integers {{Mvar|a}} and {{Mvar|b}} such that <math>a p^k + b q^k = 1.</math> This yields a contradiction, as

: <math>1 = |1|_* \leq |a|_* |p|_*^k + |b|_* |q|_*^k < \frac{|a|_* + |b|_*}{2} \leq 1.</math>

This means that there exists a unique prime {{Mvar|p}} such that <math>|p|_* < 1</math> and that for all other primes {{Mvar|q}}, one has <math>|q|_* = 1</math> (from the hypothesis of this second case). Let <math>\lambda = -\log_p |p|_*</math>. From <math>|p|_* < 1</math>, we infer that <math>0 < \lambda < \infty</math>. (And indeed in this case, all positive <math>\lambda</math> give absolute values equivalent to the p-adic one.)

We finally verify that <math>|p|_p^\lambda = p^{-\lambda} = |p|_*</math> and that for all other primes {{Mvar|q}}, <math>|q|_p^\lambda = 1 = |q|_*</math>. As per the above result on the determination of an absolute value by its values on the prime numbers, we conclude that <math>|r|_* = |r|_p^{\lambda}</math> for all rational {{Mvar|r}}, implying that this absolute value is equivalent to the {{mvar|p}}-adic one. [[Q.E.D.|<math>\blacksquare</math>]]

== Another Ostrowski's theorem ==
Another theorem states that any field, complete with respect to an [[absolute value (algebra)#Types of absolute value|Archimedean absolute value]], is (algebraically and topologically) isomorphic to either the [[real numbers]] or the [[complex numbers]]. This is sometimes also referred to as Ostrowski's theorem.<ref>Cassels (1986) p. 33</ref>
